question: What first drew you to hospitality and tourism management?
lookingFor: A specific, personal origin story that shows genuine pull toward the industry, not a vague love of travel.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or experience, not a general fondness for travel
Connect it to what the industry actually involves — service, operations, people
Show it has led to sustained interest, not a one-off impression
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I worked a summer job at the front desk of a small family-run hotel, and what hooked me wasn't the glamour, it was watching the manager solve a double-booking crisis calmly while keeping the guest smiling. That mix of pressure, logistics, and people skills was more interesting to me than any classroom subject. Since then I've read about revenue management and shadowed a local tour operator to see the other side of the industry. It confirmed this isn't a passing interest, it's genuinely how I want to spend my working life.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love traveling' with nothing about the industry itself
Describing hospitality as easy or purely fun
No evidence of sustained interest beyond one holiday
followUps: What part of that experience surprised you most?

question: Why do you want to study Hospitality & Tourism Management specifically at this university?
lookingFor: Specific knowledge of the course structure, placements, or faculty, tied to a personal goal.

bullets: Name a specific feature of the course — placement year, a module, an industry partnership
Link it to a personal goal or gap you want to fill
Show you compared it to alternatives and chose deliberately
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course stood out because of the mandatory industry placement year built into second year, which is rare compared to other programs I looked at that treat placements as optional extras. I want that structured exposure because I've only seen the front-of-house side of the industry and I know operations and revenue management are where I'm weakest. I also looked at the events management elective, since I ran fundraising events at school and want to formalize that interest. It felt like the course that would stretch me rather than just confirm what I already know.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any hospitality program
Citing only league table rankings
Not knowing the actual course structure
followUps: What would you want to get out of the placement year specifically?

question: Have you had any part-time work or work experience in hospitality, retail, or customer service? What did you learn?
lookingFor: A concrete example with reflection on skills gained, even from a modest role.

bullets: Describe the actual role and responsibilities briefly
Pull out a specific lesson about service, teamwork, or pressure
Connect the lesson to why it matters for hospitality management
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've worked weekends at a café for the last year and a half, mostly on the till and helping with table service during rushes. The biggest lesson was that consistency matters more than individual moments of brilliance, a regular customer cares more about getting their usual order right every time than one dazzling interaction. It also taught me to read the room, knowing when someone wants a chat and when they just want their coffee fast. I think that instinct for reading guests is exactly what the industry runs on.

commonMistakes: Listing duties with no reflection on what was learned
Dismissing the job as unimportant or beneath the course
Vague claims like 'I learned teamwork' with no specifics
followUps: Tell me about a difficult customer you had to handle.

question: What have you read or followed recently about the hospitality or tourism industry?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine, ongoing engagement with industry news or trends beyond the course reading list.

bullets: Name a specific source, article, or trend, not a vague 'I keep up with the news'
Explain the content accurately and in your own words
Offer a personal opinion or reaction to it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following coverage of overtourism in places like Venice and Barcelona, particularly the debate around visitor caps and tourist taxes. I read a piece explaining how Barcelona's approach tries to balance local resident wellbeing against the revenue tourism brings, and it made me realize how much of this field is really about managing competing interests, not just filling rooms. My instinct is that destinations need to price and cap access more deliberately, but I can see the argument that this risks hurting small businesses that depend on volume. It's the kind of trade-off I want to understand properly.

commonMistakes: Naming a source but showing no real understanding of its content
Only mentioning glossy travel content with no industry substance
Having no answer at all
followUps: Do you think tourist taxes are the right solution? Why or why not?

question: How would you explain the difference between the hospitality industry and the tourism industry?
lookingFor: A clear conceptual distinction with the overlap acknowledged, showing basic subject literacy.

bullets: Define hospitality as the provision of accommodation, food, and service to guests
Define tourism as the broader movement and activity of people traveling away from home
Explain that hospitality sits as one major sector within the wider tourism system
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Hospitality is really about the direct provision of service to guests, hotels, restaurants, and events, the experience of being looked after once you arrive somewhere. Tourism is the bigger picture, it covers why and how people travel in the first place, including transport, attractions, and destination marketing. Hospitality businesses are often the biggest part of what a tourist actually experiences, so the two overlap constantly, but tourism is the wider system and hospitality is one crucial sector inside it. I think that's why the course pairs them, you can't really understand one without the other.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as identical
Giving examples only, with no actual definition
Missing the overlap between the two sectors
followUps: Can you give an example of a business that sits in both sectors at once?

question: What part of the hospitality or tourism industry do you see yourself working in after graduating?
lookingFor: A grounded, researched direction with awareness of what the role actually entails, while staying open to change.

bullets: Name a specific sector or role, not just 'hotels' in general
Show realistic understanding of what that role involves day to day
Acknowledge flexibility, since interests often shift during study
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to event and conference management, I like the idea of coordinating lots of moving parts toward one live outcome, which I got a taste of running school events. I understand it involves a lot of vendor negotiation, budgeting, and problem-solving under time pressure, not just the creative side people imagine. That said, I know the course and placement year might pull me toward something I haven't considered yet, like destination marketing, and I'm genuinely open to that. What matters most to me is staying in a role where I'm coordinating people and experiences rather than sitting purely behind a desk.

commonMistakes: An overly vague answer like 'I just want to work in hotels'
A plan so rigid it ignores what the course might reveal
No understanding of what the named role actually involves
followUps: What skills do you think you'd need to develop most for that role?

question: A guest at a hotel complains loudly in the lobby that their room isn't ready two hours after check-in time. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: A calm, structured approach to service recovery that balances the guest's experience with operational reality.

bullets: Prioritize moving the guest away from a public scene and listening first
Offer a concrete interim solution, not just an apology
Follow up with a genuine gesture once the issue is resolved
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd first invite them somewhere quieter, a public argument makes it worse for both the guest and other visitors watching. I'd listen properly before explaining anything, because most people just want to feel heard before they want a solution. Then I'd offer something concrete right away, like storing their bags and giving them a voucher for the lounge while the room is finished, rather than just apologizing with nothing practical attached. Once they're checked in I'd follow up personally, maybe a small upgrade or a note, so the last impression isn't the wait but how it was handled.

commonMistakes: Only offering an apology with no practical action
Getting defensive or blaming other departments in front of the guest
Ignoring the emotional side and jumping straight to logistics
followUps: What would you do if the room still wasn't ready an hour later?

question: What do you understand by sustainable tourism, and can you give an example?
lookingFor: An accurate grasp of the concept covering environmental, economic, and social dimensions, with a concrete example.

bullets: Define sustainable tourism as balancing environmental, economic, and community impact, not just 'being green'
Give a specific real or plausible example
Show awareness that sustainability can involve trade-offs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sustainable tourism means managing travel so it doesn't damage the environment, local economy, or community that hosts it, and that's broader than just recycling or reducing plastic. Costa Rica is the example I know best, they've built a lot of their tourism brand around ecotourism, using park entry fees to directly fund conservation while also creating jobs for local guides. What I find interesting is that it isn't purely altruistic, sustainability there is also a competitive advantage because it's become part of the country's identity. I think that's the realistic case for sustainability, it has to make business sense too or it won't last.

commonMistakes: Reducing sustainability to just environmental issues, ignoring community and economy
No concrete example, only abstract definitions
Treating sustainability as purely a cost with no business upside
followUps: Do you think mass tourism and sustainability can ever really coexist?

question: What do you think is the biggest challenge facing the hospitality or tourism industry right now?
lookingFor: An informed, specific view of a real current challenge with some reasoning, not a generic worry.

bullets: Name a specific, current challenge, such as staffing shortages, sustainability, or shifting demand patterns
Explain why it matters with a bit of evidence or reasoning
Offer a personal view or possible response, even a partial one
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think staffing is the biggest issue, a lot of hotels and restaurants are still struggling to fill roles after the pandemic pushed people out of the industry, and pay and working hours haven't always caught up to make it attractive again. That matters because service quality depends entirely on having enough trained people, you can't automate away the human side of a good stay. I don't think there's an easy fix, but I've read that some chains are trying better career progression paths and more flexible shift patterns to make roles feel less like dead ends. It's part of why I'm interested in the management side, because I think leadership decisions are exactly what determines whether that works.

commonMistakes: A vague answer like 'competition' with no specifics
Naming an issue without explaining why it matters
Sounding like it was memorized rather than reasoned through
followUps: How do you think technology could help or hurt that problem?

question: What would you bring to a class full of other hospitality and tourism students?
lookingFor: A specific, credible strength or perspective, not a generic list of positive traits.

bullets: Name a specific trait or experience, backed by an example
Explain how it would actually help group work or discussion
Avoid sounding boastful or disconnected from the course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I'd bring a practical, ground-level perspective, since I've spent two years actually working service shifts rather than just studying the theory from outside. When we discuss things like service recovery or staffing in seminars, I can offer what it actually feels like on a busy Saturday night, not just the textbook version. I also tend to ask the awkward follow-up question in group discussions, which I think keeps conversations honest rather than settling for the easy answer. I'd rather contribute that kind of grounded pushback than just agree with whatever the room lands on first.

commonMistakes: A list of adjectives with no evidence
Overselling to the point of sounding arrogant
An answer unrelated to hospitality or teamwork
followUps: Can you give an example of when you pushed back on a group's first answer?

question: How would you handle a situation where a guest's cultural expectations conflict with your hotel's standard service practices?
lookingFor: Nuanced reasoning that respects cultural difference without abandoning consistent standards, showing genuine cross-cultural awareness.

bullets: Acknowledge the tension honestly rather than dismissing either side
Describe how you'd seek to understand the specific need before acting
Show a willingness to adapt where reasonable while explaining limits clearly and respectfully
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by trying to understand exactly what the guest needs and why, rather than assuming I already know based on a general idea of their culture, because that can be its own mistake. If it's something we can reasonably accommodate, like dietary arrangements or a request around room setup, I'd try to make it happen even if it's outside our usual process. If it genuinely conflicts with something like a safety regulation or a policy we can't bend, I'd explain the reason clearly and respectfully rather than just saying no. I think the real skill is treating it as a specific person's need rather than a stereotype, and being honest about where flexibility ends.

commonMistakes: Assuming cultural norms based on stereotypes rather than asking
Treating all requests as either fully accommodated or flatly refused
Avoiding the tension entirely instead of engaging with it
followUps: Can you think of a real example, from travel or reading, where this kind of conflict came up?

question: A restaurant's costs are mostly fixed, like rent, but its revenue depends on how many covers it serves each night. Why does that make occupancy or footfall so important to hospitality businesses?
lookingFor: Basic grasp of fixed versus variable costs and how thin margins make volume and utilization critical in hospitality.

bullets: Explain that fixed costs like rent and staff don't change much whether the restaurant is full or empty
Show that revenue only comes in when covers or rooms are filled, so low volume still leaves the fixed costs to pay
Connect this to why the industry is so focused on occupancy rates and yield management
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If rent, base staffing, and utilities stay roughly the same whether the restaurant serves ten covers or eighty, then every table filled is doing more work to cover those fixed costs before any profit is made. An empty table on a Tuesday night is a cost that's already been paid for and just wasn't recovered. That's why I think hotels and restaurants care so much about things like dynamic pricing and off-peak promotions, they're really trying to smooth out demand so fixed costs get covered more consistently rather than depending on a few busy nights to carry the whole week.

commonMistakes: Confusing fixed and variable costs
Not connecting the concept to real hospitality practices like yield management
Giving a purely abstract answer with no restaurant example
followUps: What strategies have you seen businesses use to fill quiet periods?

question: This industry often involves long, irregular hours and high-pressure peak periods. Why do you think you'd cope well with that?
lookingFor: Realistic self-assessment backed by a concrete example of handling pressure, not just a confident claim.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly that the demands are real, not romanticize them
Give a specific past example of coping with pressure or irregular hours
Explain what personally sustains you through that kind of work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I won't pretend it's easy, I've done enough weekend shifts to know that a packed Saturday night leaves you exhausted in a way a normal day doesn't. But I've noticed I actually work better under that kind of pressure, during a busy brunch rush I found myself getting more focused rather than flustered, prioritizing the next table instead of getting overwhelmed by all of them at once. What keeps me going through the long hours is genuinely liking the pace, the day goes fast and I get a real sense of having done something concrete by the end of a shift. I know a full career of it is a bigger test than one summer job, which is part of why I want the placement year to properly stress-test that.

commonMistakes: Claiming pressure is no problem with no evidence
Romanticizing the hours as glamorous rather than demanding
No specific example of past pressure handled well
followUps: Tell me about a specific shift or day where the pressure really tested you.

question: How is technology changing the way hotels or travel companies operate, and do you see that as mostly positive?
lookingFor: Awareness of real technology trends in the sector with a balanced, considered view rather than blanket enthusiasm or dismissal.

bullets: Name specific technology, like mobile check-in, dynamic pricing algorithms, or online travel agents
Discuss a genuine benefit and a genuine downside or risk
Land on a considered personal view rather than a flat yes or no
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Mobile check-in and keyless room entry are probably the most visible changes, they cut queuing time and give guests more control over their own arrival. Online travel agents have also completely reshaped how hotels get booked, which is efficient for guests but has squeezed hotel margins through commission fees and made properties more dependent on platforms they don't control. I think it's mostly positive for convenience, but I do worry it can strip out the personal moments that make hospitality distinctive in the first place, if every interaction becomes an app, you lose the chance for a staff member to actually notice and respond to a guest. My honest view is that the best use of technology is removing friction from logistics so staff have more time for the human parts, not replacing the human parts altogether.

commonMistakes: Treating all technology change as purely good with no downside
No specific examples, just general statements about 'technology'
Ignoring the guest experience side entirely and focusing only on business efficiency
followUps: Can you think of a hospitality technology that actually made service worse?

question: Think about a destination you'd love to visit. What do you think makes a place successful at attracting tourists?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of destination marketing factors, drawn from a real example, not just personal taste.

bullets: Name a specific destination and what genuinely draws visitors there
Identify concrete factors, like accessibility, infrastructure, marketing, or unique attractions
Show awareness that appeal has to be actively managed, not just natural
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd love to visit Kyoto, and I think what makes it so successful is that it combines something genuinely unique, the temples and traditional districts, with really practical accessibility through Japan's rail network. It's also carefully marketed and managed, seasonal things like cherry blossom timing get built into how the city promotes itself, which shows real destination planning rather than luck. I think a lot of places have interesting history or scenery but fail to attract tourists because they lack the infrastructure or marketing to make visiting easy and appealing. It made me realize that a destination's success is as much about management decisions as it is about what's naturally there.

commonMistakes: Only describing personal taste with no analysis of why it attracts tourists broadly
Ignoring accessibility or infrastructure factors entirely
Treating destination appeal as purely natural, with no mention of active management or marketing
followUps: What would you change about how that destination manages its tourism?

question: Tell me about a time you led or coordinated a team, even informally. What did you learn about managing people?
lookingFor: A concrete leadership example with genuine reflection on what makes people work well together.

bullets: Describe a specific, real situation of leading or coordinating others
Explain the actual challenge in managing the people involved, not just the task
Draw out a genuine lesson about motivation, communication, or delegation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I coordinated the setup crew for our school's end-of-year event, which meant organizing about fifteen people with very different levels of motivation. I learned quickly that just assigning tasks wasn't enough, some people needed a clear deadline and to be checked on, while others worked better if I just explained why a task mattered and left them to it. The hardest part was one volunteer who kept disappearing, and I found that pulling them aside privately worked far better than calling it out in front of the group. It taught me that managing people is really about reading what each person responds to, not applying one leadership style to everyone.

commonMistakes: Describing only the task, with nothing about managing people
Claiming leadership success with no acknowledgment of difficulty
A generic answer with no real, specific incident
followUps: How did you handle the team member who wasn't pulling their weight?

question: How would you make sure a hospitality business is welcoming to guests with different needs, for example a guest with a disability or an elderly traveler?
lookingFor: Practical awareness of accessibility considerations beyond box-ticking compliance, with genuine empathy.

bullets: Mention concrete practical measures, like accessible rooms, clear signage, or staff training
Show that accessibility is about dignity and independence, not just physical compliance
Recognize that asking the guest directly is often better than assuming their needs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start with the practical basics, step-free access, accessible bathrooms, and staff who actually know where those rooms are rather than guests having to explain their own needs on arrival. But I think the deeper issue is dignity, an elderly guest or a guest with a disability doesn't want to feel like a special case being managed, they want the same independence as anyone else. That means training staff to ask rather than assume, someone might use a wheelchair and need zero extra help at breakfast, while someone else might need something completely different. I'd rather build a culture of asking good questions than a checklist that assumes one type of need covers everyone.

commonMistakes: Reducing accessibility to only physical ramps or compliance requirements
Assuming what a guest needs rather than asking
Treating the topic as a box to check rather than a genuine guest experience issue
followUps: Have you had any experience, personal or observed, that shaped this view?

question: Many tourism businesses are highly seasonal. What challenges does that create, and how might a business address them?
lookingFor: Understanding of the practical business impact of seasonality, with at least one plausible mitigation strategy.

bullets: Explain the core problem, revenue and staffing swings between peak and off-peak periods
Give a concrete example of a business affected by seasonality
Suggest a realistic mitigation, like off-season pricing, diversifying offerings, or targeting different markets
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Seasonality creates a real staffing headache, a ski resort might need triple the staff in winter but can't justify keeping them all on payroll in summer, so businesses lose experienced people every year and have to retrain constantly. It also puts pressure on cash flow, since a huge share of annual revenue has to be earned in just a few months. I've read about resorts trying to fix this by diversifying into summer activities like mountain biking or hosting conferences in the off-season, essentially building a second peak to smooth out the year. I think that kind of creative repositioning is more sustainable than just discounting heavily, because deep discounts can damage the brand's value over time.

commonMistakes: Only naming the problem with no discussion of a solution
Vague answer with no real business example
Ignoring staffing impact and focusing only on revenue
followUps: Can you think of a destination or business that handles this particularly well?

question: As a hotel duty manager, you discover the property is overbooked tonight and one guest with a confirmed reservation will need to be turned away or relocated. How would you decide who that is and how would you handle it?
lookingFor: Structured, fair reasoning about a genuinely difficult operational and ethical trade-off, with attention to how it's communicated.

bullets: Acknowledge there's no fully painless option and reason through fair criteria rather than picking arbitrarily
Consider practical criteria like loyalty status, length of stay, or how late they are due to check in, while being honest that any rule feels unfair to someone
Emphasize how the decision is communicated, proactively and with a genuine gesture of goodwill, not left until the guest is standing at the desk
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd first try to solve it without anyone losing out, checking if any guests can be upgraded elsewhere or if a nearby partner hotel has space, since that avoids the ethical problem outright. If it's unavoidable, I'd look at reasonable criteria like who booked most recently versus who has a long-standing reservation, rather than something arbitrary, and I'd be honest with myself that no rule will feel fair to the person affected. The part I'd focus on most is how it's communicated, calling the guest before they arrive rather than surprising them at the desk, explaining clearly, and offering a genuinely good alternative like a comparable room elsewhere plus transport and a rate adjustment. I think how you handle the bad news often matters as much as the decision itself.

commonMistakes: Picking a guest to relocate with no stated reasoning
Focusing only on solving it logistically with no thought for how it's communicated
Assuming overbooking is purely a guest's bad luck with no business responsibility
followUps: What would you say to that guest face to face?

question: This industry often involves working with people from many different countries and backgrounds. Do you speak any other languages, or how have you handled communicating across a language barrier before?
lookingFor: Genuine reflection on cross-cultural communication skills, whether through language ability or a real problem-solving example.

bullets: Mention actual language ability honestly, without overstating fluency
Give a concrete example of communicating despite a language or cultural gap
Show a practical, resourceful attitude toward the barrier rather than treating it as a wall
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I speak conversational Spanish and basic French, nothing fluent, but enough to get through simple exchanges. What I found more useful was during my café job, where I once had a group of tourists with almost no shared English, and I ended up using a mix of simple words, gestures, and a translation app on my phone to get their order right. It took longer, but I noticed that just staying patient and smiling through the confusion actually built more trust than rushing would have. I think that resourcefulness, being willing to find a way rather than getting flustered, is more important in this industry than being fluent in ten languages.

commonMistakes: Overstating language fluency that wouldn't hold up under follow-up
Treating a language barrier as a dead end with no example of solving it
Giving a dismissive answer implying language skills don't matter
followUps: Which language would you most want to improve for this career, and why?

subtopic: Understanding hospitality vs other business degrees
question: Why hospitality and tourism management specifically, rather than a general business degree?
lookingFor: Clear reasoning for choosing the specialized route over a generalist one, grounded in real interest in the sector.

bullets: Acknowledge honestly what a general business degree offers
Explain what the specialization adds that generalist study wouldn't
Show the choice reflects genuine commitment to the sector, not just a narrower path
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A general business degree would give me solid foundations in finance, marketing, and strategy, and I did seriously consider it. But I want those concepts taught through the lens of an industry I already care about, understanding yield management or brand strategy specifically as they apply to a hotel or a tour operator, not as abstract case studies from unrelated sectors. I also want the practical exposure this route offers, the placement year and industry-specific modules like events or destination management aren't things a general degree would give me. It felt like choosing depth in a field I'm genuinely committed to over breadth in a field I'm not sure I'd stay in.

commonMistakes: Dismissing general business degrees unfairly
No real reasoning, just stating a preference
Sounding unsure whether they actually want the specialization
followUps: What would you do if you later realized you preferred the general business side?

question: A hotel receives a harsh, detailed negative review online about the service. As a manager, how would you respond?
lookingFor: A measured, professional approach to reputation management that treats the complaint as useful information, not just a threat.

bullets: Emphasize responding calmly and professionally rather than defensively
Distinguish between acknowledging the guest publicly and investigating the specifics internally
Show the review can be used constructively to fix a real operational issue
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd respond publicly but briefly, acknowledging their experience and apologizing without getting defensive or trying to argue the details in the comments, since that rarely looks good to other readers. Behind the scenes, I'd actually investigate what happened rather than assuming the review is exaggerated, checking with the staff involved and looking at whether it points to a pattern rather than a one-off. If it turns out to be a genuine gap, understaffing at breakfast, say, I'd treat the review as free feedback rather than just damage control, and try to fix the actual cause. I think guests can usually tell the difference between a hotel that's genuinely listening and one that's just managing its image.

commonMistakes: Suggesting arguing publicly with the reviewer
Treating the review purely as a PR problem with no interest in the underlying issue
Dismissing the review as probably unfair without investigating
followUps: What would you do if you found the review was genuinely unfair or exaggerated?

question: Can you describe a time you noticed a small detail that made a big difference to someone's experience?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific example showing an instinct for the small, thoughtful touches that define good service.

bullets: Describe a specific, small, concrete detail, not a grand gesture
Explain how noticing it changed the outcome for the other person
Connect it to why small details matter disproportionately in hospitality
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During a shift at the café I noticed a regular customer always ordered the same coffee but seemed a bit down one morning, so I mentioned I'd remembered his order and asked how his week was going. It turned out he'd just had a rough time at work, and he actually thanked me on his way out for making him feel noticed rather than just served. It was such a small thing on my end, but it clearly mattered more to him than the coffee itself. That's what convinced me hospitality isn't really about the product, it's about whether someone feels seen, and that comes from paying attention to small details most people would miss.

commonMistakes: Describing a large gesture rather than a genuinely small detail
No clear outcome or impact on the other person
A generic, unconvincing anecdote that sounds rehearsed
followUps: How do you train yourself to notice details like that consistently?

question: How do you think travel habits have changed since the pandemic, and what does that mean for the industry going forward?
lookingFor: Informed, specific analysis of a real post-pandemic shift with reasoned implications for businesses.

bullets: Name a specific, real behavioral shift, such as remote-work-enabled longer stays or a preference for flexible booking
Explain the underlying cause of that shift, not just describe it
Draw a reasoned implication for how businesses need to adapt
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One clear shift is the rise of what's often called bleisure travel, people extending business trips or combining remote work with longer stays somewhere pleasant, since flexible and hybrid work made that possible in a way it wasn't before. I think that's driven hotels to think differently about amenities, better in-room wifi and workspaces matter more now than they used to for a business traveler. I've also noticed people booking with more flexible cancellation terms, since the pandemic made everyone more wary of rigid non-refundable plans. For the industry, I think that means less predictable, shorter-lead-time booking patterns, which puts more pressure on revenue management systems to price dynamically rather than relying on old seasonal patterns.

commonMistakes: A vague statement that 'travel changed' with no specific trend named
Describing a trend without explaining the underlying cause
No connection to practical implications for hospitality businesses
followUps: Do you think that trend will still hold in five years, or was it temporary?

question: This industry has a reputation for high staff turnover, especially among graduates who leave within a few years. What makes you confident you'd stay committed to it long term?
lookingFor: Honest engagement with the industry's real retention challenge, backed by a specific, credible personal reason for staying.

bullets: Acknowledge the reputation honestly rather than denying it exists
Give a specific personal reason tied to what genuinely motivates them, not a generic assurance
Show awareness of what commonly drives people out, and why their own situation differs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know the reputation is real, a lot of graduates leave after a couple of years because the entry-level hours and pay don't match what they expected, especially if they went in only chasing the glamorous side of the industry. What makes me different, I think, is that I've already done the unglamorous version of the work through my café job, the early mornings and difficult customers, and I still want more of it rather than less. I'm also drawn to the management and strategy side long term, not just service roles, so I see a clear progression I actually want rather than a dead end. I'd rather go in with realistic expectations now than get disillusioned in year two.

commonMistakes: Denying the industry has a turnover problem at all
A generic reassurance with no personal grounding
Sounding naive about how demanding entry-level roles actually are
followUps: What would make you consider leaving the industry, if anything?
